title: Implement integrated farm layout and site selection

lessons.title: Site selection for farm enterprises and infrastructure
lessons.html:
Why site selection matters

Where an enterprise or structure is placed determines production potential, operating costs, environmental impact and risk for decades. A packhouse built in a flood zone, an orchard planted in a frost pocket, or a piggery upwind of the farm village creates problems that are expensive or impossible to fix later.

Site assessment criteria

FactorWhat to assess
ClimateRainfall, frost risk and frost pockets, heat units, chill units, hail, wind
Soil and land capabilityDepth, texture, drainage, pH and fertility, slope, erosion risk
WaterQuantity and reliability, quality, legal entitlement under the National Water Act 36 of 1998, distance to water source
TopographySlope for drainage and machinery, aspect (north-facing slopes are warmer in South Africa), flood lines
Access and servicesRoads, all-weather access for trucks, electricity, telecommunications
Markets and inputsDistance to buyers, packhouses, abattoirs, input suppliers
EnvironmentWetlands, rivers, protected vegetation, neighbours, odour and noise impacts
Legal and zoningLand use rights, environmental authorisations where required, building plans, biosecurity requirements
SecurityTheft risk, visibility, fencing needs

Enterprise-specific needs

  • Orchards: deep, well-drained soils, good air drainage to avoid frost, adequate chill or heat units for the cultivar, irrigation water.
  • Vegetables under irrigation: level, fertile land near water and packing facilities.
  • Intensive livestock (poultry, pigs, feedlots, dairy): elevated, well-drained sites, away from watercourses and housing, downwind of homes, with biosecurity zoning and manure management.
  • Extensive grazing: land unsuited to cropping, with water point distribution.
  • Tunnels and greenhouses: level, sheltered from strong winds, good light and water.

lessons.title: Designing and implementing an integrated layout
lessons.html:
Integration principles

An integrated layout arranges all enterprises, infrastructure and natural areas so they work together efficiently and sustainably.

  • Workflow efficiency: minimise distances between related activities, such as the packhouse close to the orchards, the feed store close to the dairy, the workshop near the main roads.
  • Resource cycling: place manure sources near cropping lands or compost sites; use crop residues as feed where appropriate.
  • Water by gravity: locate reservoirs high on the farm where possible to reduce pumping.
  • Conservation: keep slopes, wetlands and riparian zones under cover; plan contours, waterways and buffer strips; link natural areas as corridors.
  • Safety and hygiene: chemical and fuel stores away from water, housing and food handling; biosecurity zones around livestock units; clean and dirty traffic routes separated.
  • Camp design: camp sizes matched to herd size and rotation plan; water points shared between camps; gates in corners near water to ease movement.
  • Future expansion: leave space for growth.

Developing the layout plan

  1. Produce a base map using aerial or satellite imagery, with boundaries, contours and existing features.
  2. Overlay soil and land capability maps.
  3. Mark constraints: wetlands, flood lines, steep slopes, servitudes, power lines.
  4. Allocate land uses to suitable areas.
  5. Position infrastructure: roads, buildings, water systems, fences, handling facilities.
  6. Check against the criteria and consult specialists, such as soil scientists, engineers and environmental practitioners.
  7. Obtain approvals required for water use, environmental impacts or buildings.

Implementation

  • Phase the work according to priority and budget.
  • Build conservation structures and roads before planting where possible.
  • Set out lines using surveying equipment or GPS.
  • Supervise contractors against specifications.
  • Update the farm map as changes are made.

Evaluation

Review the layout periodically: travel times, water distribution problems, erosion, production results and safety incidents show where improvements are needed.

Key points

  • Assess climate, soil, water, topography, access, markets, environment and legal factors.
  • Match each enterprise to a site that suits its specific needs.
  • Integrate for workflow, resource cycling, conservation and safety.
  • Build the layout on maps, constraints and specialist input, with required approvals.
  • Implement in phases and review the layout over time.
